scenario: AITA for not giving my wife what she wants to eat? | I will try to keep this as concise as possible. My wife and I have been together for going on 27 years. We met at a pretty low point in both of our lives, coming from broken homes and an unhealthy dependency on food. We both probably weighed around 300lbs, and though our weight has fluctuated over the years we both currently sit at around 350lbs and 450lbs respectively, with her being the latter. I cook all the food that we eat as my wife is unable to be on her feet long enough to make meals. I am completely okay with this, as I’ve really been able to hone in on my cooking skills over the years and can essentially throw down in the kitchen. When my oldest daughter told us she was pregnant a few months back, it really made me reevaluate our lifestyle choices. I wanna be able to run around with my grandkids, but I can’t do that in my current situation. Over the course of several months I’ve been looking into healthier alternatives of our favorite foods and trying to exercise more, slowly implementing both into our lives and my wife was initially on board. More recently she’s stopped wanting to workout with me which I respected, but I’ve continued to cook healthier meals and she no longer wants to eat them. I’ve stopped buying junk and with a suspended license she can’t drive to get fast food, so I assumed she would just eat what I made like she always has. She feels like I’m forcing a lifestyle into her that she never agreed to, but I’m not pushing her to eat what I’ve made or workout. I suggested she could learn to cook what she wants and I would even help her, but I won’t continue to cook foods I no longer want to eat. Does this make me TA?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the person in this scenario is "AITA" (Ask if it's a good idea to do something) or "TA" (Toxic). Let me break it down step by step. First, the person has been married for 27 years, which is a long time. Both came from broken homes and had an unhealthy dependency on food, leading them to be overweight. The husband cooks all the meals because his wife can't stand for long enough to cook. He's proud of his cooking skills and has been making healthier alternatives to their favorite foods. He also started exercising more after his daughter got pregnant, wanting to be active with his grandkids. Initially, his wife was on board with the healthier lifestyle, but lately, she's stopped working out with him and doesn't want to eat the healthier meals he's preparing. She feels like he's forcing a lifestyle change on her without her agreement. The husband, however, says he's not pushing her to eat what he makes or work out. He suggested she could learn to cook what she wants, even offering to help, but he won't continue cooking foods he doesn't want to eat anymore. So, is he in the wrong here? Let's consider the dynamics. The husband is taking initiative to improve their health, which is positive. He's been cooking for a long time, so it's understandable he doesn't want to continue making unhealthy food. However, his wife feels forced into this change, which is a problem. He says he's not pushing her, but by stopping the purchase of junk food and not making the meals she wants, he's limiting her options. Since she can't drive due to a suspended license, she can't get fast food herself. This might make her feel trapped, leading to resentment. On the other hand, he's trying to take responsibility for his health and set a good example. He's also offering to help her learn to cook, which is a supportive gesture. But the way he's implementing the changes might be coming off as controlling, even if he doesn't intend it that way. I think the key here is communication. He needs to discuss his concerns and desires with his wife without making her feel forced. It's important to find a middle ground where both their needs are considered. Maybe they can compromise on some healthier meals that she still enjoys, or find other ways for her to get the foods she wants without him having to prepare them. In conclusion, while his intentions are good, the approach might be making his wife feel pressured. Better communication and compromise could help both of them feel respected and supported in their health journeys.
